item.source_title: Fil Hunter, Steven Biver & Paul Fuqua, Light: Science & Magic, 5th Edition (Focal Press), chapters beyond ch. 3
item.source_locator: Ch. 7 'The Case of the Disappearing Glass', section 'Secondary Opaque Subjects'
item.question: A labelled glass bottle has to look premium and its label has to be legible. The lighting that gives the bottle its describing highlight puts a sheen across the paper. Work through the book's options and say which it rules out and why.
item.answer: The conflict is real and the book states it: most of a paper's reflection is diffuse but some is direct, so the light producing the direct reflection on the glass is also likely to obscure the label. Two remedies work. Move the offending light higher, so the label's direct reflection goes downward instead of toward the lens. Or, where good highlight placement forbids moving the light, interpose a small opaque card blocking exactly the angles that produce direct reflection on the label — and its size is critical: a gobo extending beyond the label's own family of angles will itself reflect in the glass. A polarizing filter is the third option and the book rules it out in most cases: much of the desirable highlight on the glass is usually polarized already, so a polarizer that eliminates the label's reflection is also likely to interfere with the light the glass needs. Underneath all three sits the prior question the authors insist comes first — which of the two is the principal subject — and they say that cannot be settled on a technical basis at all.
item.support: Ch. 7, 'Secondary Opaque Subjects' for the three options and the gobo size constraint; 'Recognizing the Principal Subject' for the prior decision.
confounders: reaching for the polarizer first, which is the intuitive move and the one the source blocks here
oversizing the gobo, which converts a label fix into a black reflection in the glass
treating this as a legibility defect rather than as a scene lit for the wrong principal subject

item.source_title: Fil Hunter, Steven Biver & Paul Fuqua, Light: Science & Magic, 5th Edition (Focal Press), chapters beyond ch. 3
item.source_locator: Ch. 7 'The Case of the Disappearing Glass', sections 'Defining the Surface of Glassware' and 'Position the Light'
item.question: Compare a small bright highlight and a large dim one on the surface of a glass. What does the book say each does for the viewer, and what sets the difference in practice?
item.answer: They do opposite jobs. The tiny bright spots are distracting at the least and meaningless at best: they are too small and too bright to tell the viewer anything about surface detail or texture. A large highlight informs — it serves the constructive purpose of saying how the glass surface looks and feels. In practice the difference is set by how much of the relevant family of angles is filled with light, and, with a diffusion sheet, by the distance from the lamp head to the sheet: close in, only the centre of the sheet lights and the highlight is small and bright; pulled back, the whole sheet lights and reflects as a larger highlight. The authors add that the larger highlight should usually be kept dimmer, because a brightly lit whole sheet reflects as an obvious hard-edged rectangle that advertises a studio light and costs the scene its reality — and that strips of black tape on the sheet can make the reflection read as a window instead.
item.support: Ch. 7, 'Defining the Surface of Glassware', including the two matched highlight frames and the taped diffusion sheet.
confounders: assuming brighter highlights read as more premium or more glossy
attributing the difference to the size of the source alone, ignoring the lamp-to-diffuser distance
missing that the source deliberately makes the large highlight dimmer, not brighter

item.source_title: Fil Hunter, Steven Biver & Paul Fuqua, Light: Science & Magic, 5th Edition (Focal Press), chapters beyond ch. 3
item.source_locator: Ch. 7 'The Case of the Disappearing Glass', sections 'Bright-field Lighting' and 'Dark-field Lighting'
item.question: Define bright-field and dark-field lighting as this book defines them, in terms of the family of angles rather than in terms of the resulting picture.
item.answer: Both are defined by what occupies the two extreme limits of the family of angles that acts on a glass edge — the points the book labels L. Bright-field lighting requires that there be NO light at those limits, so the edge stays dark, and the glass must therefore be shown against a bright background; the authors also call it the dark-on-light approach. Dark-field lighting requires that light come from those limits and from nowhere else, so the edge is bright, and the glass must be shown against a dark background; the light-on-dark approach. The two are the same geometric fact read in opposite directions, which is why the authors call them two attractive opposites.
item.support: Ch. 7, 'Two Attractive Opposites' onward. The L-limits framing is the source's own; the two step sequences give the practical form.
confounders: defining them only by the resulting picture — dark glass on white, light glass on black — which misses that both are statements about where light may be
assuming dark-field means less light overall; it uses one very large source
supposing the whole family of angles matters, when the source says only its extreme limits do

item.source_title: Fil Hunter, Steven Biver & Paul Fuqua, Light: Science & Magic, 5th Edition (Focal Press), chapters beyond ch. 3
item.source_locator: Ch. 7 'The Case of the Disappearing Glass', section 'Liquid as a Lens'
item.question: A wine glass is photographed against a background that exactly fills the camera's frame, and the studio appears as a dark surround inside the bowl of the glass. What has happened, and why is the obvious fix barred?
item.answer: A round transparent container filled with liquid is optically a lens, and it sees a wider field than the camera does. A background large enough to fill the camera's field of view is therefore not large enough to fill the field of view seen through the liquid, so the white rectangle in the centre of the glass is the background and the dark area around it is the rest of the studio. The obvious fix — a larger background, or one moved closer to increase its effective size — is barred because a background larger than the field of view extends into the family of angles acting on the glass edge and sacrifices the edge definition the whole chapter exists to protect. The book's remedy is to move the CAMERA closer and, if necessary, fit a shorter lens to hold the image size, so the existing background fills the area seen through the liquid. The stated cost is increased perspective distortion, visible as a deeper ellipse at the rim, which may or may not be acceptable in a given scene.
item.support: Ch. 7, 'Liquid as a Lens', with the before-and-after wine-glass pair; the bar on enlarging the background comes from 'Position the Camera' earlier in the chapter.
confounders: enlarging or approaching the background, which is the natural move and the one the source rules out
assuming the dark surround is a vignetting or exposure problem
forgetting that the remedy costs perspective, which the source states plainly

item.source_title: Fil Hunter, Steven Biver & Paul Fuqua, Light: Science & Magic, 5th Edition (Focal Press), chapters beyond ch. 3
item.question: A metal box stands on a sheet of clear glass. A polarizing filter on the lens turns the glass black and leaves the metal untouched. What makes the filter able to discriminate?
item.answer: The two surfaces polarize differently. Most of the direct reflection from glass viewed at that angle is polarized, so a lens polarizer can extinguish it. Direct reflection from metal is never polarized unless the light source itself is polarized, so the same filter passes it and the metal is unaffected. The filter is not selecting by object or by brightness; it is selecting by a physical property the two materials do not share. The book is careful about the boundary elsewhere: the same trick fails for a black subject on glass, because much of a black subject's direct reflection is likely to be polarized too, so the filter that clears the table would probably blacken the subject as well.
item.support: Ch. 6, 'A Transparent Background', with the before-and-after photographs; the withdrawal for black subjects is in ch. 9, 'Keeping the Subject Away from the Background'. The conductor-versus-insulator guideline behind it is chapter-3 material and already live Canon.
confounders: assuming a polarizer reduces all reflections, which is the general belief the source contradicts
attributing the discrimination to the angle rather than to the material class
generalising the trick to any dark support, which the book explicitly blocks

item.source_title: Fil Hunter, Steven Biver & Paul Fuqua, Light: Science & Magic, 5th Edition (Focal Press), chapters beyond ch. 3
item.source_locator: Ch. 7 'The Case of the Disappearing Glass', section 'The Best of Both Worlds'
item.question: A photographer puts a set of glassware inside a white tent to get rid of the studio reflections, and the glass loses its outline entirely. Explain the failure using the book's own account, and say what it prescribes for a frame that genuinely needs both fields.
item.answer: The tent removed the extraneous reflections and removed the edges with them. The part of the tent the camera saw became a light background, while the rest of the tent lit the glass — which is the light-on-light combination, and the one arrangement that cannot define an edge, because edge definition requires a tonal difference between the edge and the ground immediately behind it. The book attributes most failures in photographing glass to using bright field and dark field simultaneously, deliberately or naively, and it names this specific case. Where a picture genuinely needs both, the prescription is not to blend them but to keep them separate: divide the scene mentally, assign one region to bright field and the other to dark field. Wherever the two remain distinct the glass is well defined; only the transition area mixes them, and there can be a noticeable loss there, so the transition should be kept small. Note also that the tent is the remedy the same book recommends for round metal — right subject, wrong subject.
item.support: Ch. 7, 'The Best of Both Worlds', which reports the tent failure and gives the divide-the-scene prescription; Ch. 6, 'Using a Tent', for the contrasting recommendation.
confounders: adding a light to 'bring back' the edges, which is the light-on-light problem again
assuming the tent was too bright or too dim; the failure is structural, not a level
carrying a metal solution to glass because both are direct reflectors

item.source_title: Fil Hunter, Steven Biver & Paul Fuqua, Light: Science & Magic, 5th Edition (Focal Press), chapters beyond ch. 3
item.source_locator: Ch. 7 'The Case of the Disappearing Glass', section 'Position the Subject and Focus the Camera'
item.question: Moving a glass closer to the camera improves its edge definition. The book insists this is not because bigger detail is easier to see. What is the actual reason?
item.answer: It is because moving the subject toward the camera also moves it AWAY from the lighted background, and the closer a subject is to a lit background the more of that background falls inside the family of angles that acts on the glass edge. Light from those angles is exactly what obscures the edge, so increasing the subject-to-background distance reduces the light reaching the edge and the outline sharpens. The authors state the wrong explanation explicitly in order to reject it, which is worth noting: the observable effect and the plausible reason for it are different things here.

item.source_locator: Ch. 7 'The Case of the Disappearing Glass', section 'Set Up a Large Light Source'
item.question: Dark-field lighting appears in the plan diagram to need light at only two points. Why is that wrong, and what does the book substitute?
item.answer: The two-point appearance is what the authors call a representational defect caused by drawing in two dimensions. In three dimensions the same reasoning demands more: a source above and behind to keep the rim bright, and on a stemmed glass yet another to illuminate the underside of the bowl. That is four large sources for one small glass, which they call unwieldy at best. They replace all of them with a single source large enough to illuminate the top, bottom and sides at once, and say its exact size is not critical — any size between ten and twenty-five times the diameter of the subject works well. It is a rare instance of a book that argues through diagrams warning the reader against one of its own.

item.source_title: Luke Sullivan, Hey Whipple, Squeeze This: The Classic Guide to Creating Great Advertising, 6th ed. (Hoboken, NJ: John Wiley & Sons, 2022)
item.source_locator: Ch. 4 'A Controlled Daydream', section 'Remember, something has to dominate the page' (spine 15)
item.question: Sullivan says every design needs a boss. Roy Grace's version, which he quotes, makes the requirement about something other than the layout. What?
item.answer: About an agreement between the makers. Grace's formulation is that there has to be a point on every page where the art director and the writer want you to start — whether the centre, the top right corner or the left — and there has to be an understanding, an agreement, and a logical reason for where you want people to look first. So the requirement is a decision taken and shared, not a property discovered afterwards. Sullivan's own version is that whether it is a big headline, a large visual or a single word floating in white space, somebody has to be the boss, and that there must be an overall visual hierarchy — an implied order of the relative importance of the elements. He restates the requirement inside the letter-or-postcard decision, which is what makes it a precondition rather than one recommendation among others.
item.support: Stated requirement, with the operational version quoted from an art director in a case-history collection. No method for establishing dominance is given beyond scale and isolation.
confounders: treating it as a rule about which element should dominate; the requirement is that one be designated, not which

confusing it with balance or composition; the claim is about reading order

item.source_locator: Ch. 4, section 'The Cultural Construction of Meaning', printed pp. 193-194
item.question: A distributor must design one key art for a film releasing simultaneously in six Indian language markets and in three diaspora territories. What does this source's account of text actually argue, and where does the argument stop being about India in 2002?
item.answer: The argument is not that posters look better without text; it is that TEXT PICKS A LANGUAGE AND PICKING A LANGUAGE CUTS THE AUDIENCE. With the scale of national and international distribution the Indian industry enjoys, 'text is seen as a cultural barrier', which is why Indian posters 'rarely use text' while contemporary Western posters carry substantial copy including review quotations acting as 'the media seal of approval'. So the reasoning transfers exactly to the case described: one artwork across nine markets is precisely the condition the convention was a response to, and every word added narrows it. What the source also supplies is what replaced the text — from the 1980s only the title and the names of the producer, director and music director, printed solely in English, because to the public those three names themselves signal the style, content and quality of the film. That second half is where the transfer stops. It depends on a star-and-credit system in which those three names carry meaning to that public, which is a fact about Indian audiences in a particular period and not a general property of names. In a diaspora territory whose audience does not hold that system, removing the text removes the signal and does not replace it, and the source says nothing about what would. Nothing here is measured either: no comparison of a text-carrying and a text-free poster is reported anywhere in the book.
item.support: 'text is seen as a cultural barrier'
item.confounders: Treating this as a minimalist design principle inverts it. The convention is a distribution constraint, and in a single-language market the constraint is absent.

item.claim: Patel states a structural contrast between two poster traditions. Contemporary Western posters present a dramatic enigma — provocative images and text giving incomplete or paradoxical information — which requires the public to see the film to resolve it, and they are supported substantially by text, including review quotations that function as "the media seal of approval," plus studio, producer and director credits that signal the film's status. Indian posters, in contrast, "rarely use text": with the scale of national and international distribution the Indian industry enjoys, "text is seen as a cultural barrier." From the 1980s onward it has been more common for only the title and the names of the producer, director and music director to appear, printed solely in English, because to the public those three figures are a marker of the style, content and quality of the film. Indian posters accordingly "convey the familiarity of the form and content of the Indian film" rather than an enigma.

mechanism.text: Text has to be read in a language, so any text narrows the poster's reach across a multilingual distribution territory. Where the distribution is wide and the audience already knows the form, the poster's job shifts from posing a question to confirming a familiar promise, and that job can be done by images and by three names.

scope.conditions: Indian film posters from the 1980s onward against contemporary Western practice. Patel notes the earlier Indian convention was different — title and star names prominently in English with Hindi and Urdu titles in smaller lettering nearby — so this too is dated.

caveats.text: the comparison is drawn between two practices as the author characterises them; no sample of Western posters is enumerated and no count is given on either side

Patel notes the cost of the change she documents: more recent designs focusing on one narrative element are 'more universally understood' but 'convey less information about the culture in which they are produced'. That trade-off is stated by the source and is the most useful part of this object

source_stated_problems: text narrows a poster's reach across a multilingual distribution territory
source_stated_remedies: carry the message in recognisable images and in the three names that index style, content and quality

item.source_locator: printed p. 24, the NHS case, 'Keep it simple'
item.question: Airey offers the NHS mark as evidence for simplicity. What does the designer actually give as his three reasons, and what does that do to the aesthetic reading of the case?
item.answer: Richard Moon's three stated reasons for keeping the design deliberately simple were: to make it easy to implement; to last as long as possible; and to avoid being attacked by the British media, which often view identity programmes of that kind as an extravagant use of public funds. Only the second is an aesthetic or design-longevity reason at all. The first is operational and the third is political — a simple mark is cheap-looking in the sense that matters when a newspaper is costing your identity programme. That complicates the case considerably as evidence for simplicity as a design virtue: the mark is simple partly for reasons that have nothing to do with how it is perceived by its audience. Airey's own framing around it is separate — the design going essentially unchanged for nearly twenty years is a testament to its success — which is a survivorship argument, using longevity as the evidence of quality and quality as the explanation of longevity.
item.support: Printed p. 24, quoting Richard Moon of Moon Brand. The saving claim in the same passage — tens of millions of pounds by the NHS's own calculations — is an outcome asserted by a party to the project with no controls.
confounders: reporting only the longevity reason and dropping the implementation and press reasons
reading the twenty-year survival as evidence that simplicity caused it
treating the NHS's own savings estimate as independent evidence

source_terms: be consistent
consistency breeds trust. Trust wins customers.
creating these guides is your responsibility
item.claim: The source treats consistency as a property of the identity's use over time, not of the mark, and assigns responsibility for it to the designer: style guides accompany many logos and creating them is the designer's job, so that anyone inside the client company who uses the design does so consistently. It states the causal chain compactly — consistency breeds trust, trust wins customers — and its historical case is the Kellogg signature, in use on the front of every cereal packet since 1906, which the source says built trust and repeat business over the years.

mechanism.text: Repetition of the same visual identity generates trust, and trust brings customers back. The source states this twice, in the tip and in the earlier reflection that "the same visual identity seen over and over generates trust, and trust makes customers come back for more."

scope.conditions: identities used by multiple people inside a client organisation over a long period

caveats.text: the trust-to-customers chain is asserted with no evidence; Kellogg is a survivorship case with a century of confounded marketing spend behind it
the responsibility claim is a professional norm the author advocates, not an observation

source_stated_problems: inconsistent use of the identity by people inside the client's company
source_stated_remedies: create a style guide showing how to use and how not to use the design

positive.description: the Kellogg signature, used since 1906, now in a stylised red version
JCJ Architecture: the refined identity establishes consistency and allows flexibility across brochures, offset print and office laser printing

counter.description: a low-resolution 'save for web' logo file scaled up and used on the cover of a printed sales manual — named as an extreme example that defeats the purpose of hiring a specialist

intra_source_relations.note: the number of people who will use the identity is a briefing question
the JCJ refinement is offered as an instance of consistency preserved across print methods

source_terms: people usually choose products based on their perceived value rather than their actual value
the same visual identity seen over and over generates trust, and trust makes customers come back for more
item.claim: The premise the whole book rests on, stated in its second chapter: people usually choose products on perceived rather than actual value. The illustration is a celebrity driving an Aston Martin rather than a Škoda, which the source concedes is consistently rated car of the year in many European countries and offers much better mileage at a significantly cheaper price — the logical choice — while the Aston Martin identity, evoking luxury and status, usually takes the sale. The consequence the source draws is that with branding, companies can raise the perceived value of their product and build relationships that span ages and borders.

mechanism.text: Repetition of a single visual identity generates trust; trust brings customers back; perceived value therefore accrues to the identity rather than to the product's measurable attributes. The source states this chain in the chapter's closing reflection.

scope.conditions: consumer purchase decisions; the source's cases are cars, cereal and juice

caveats.text: this is the source's position, not a finding. No evidence, no citation, no measurement; the Aston Martin / Škoda contrast is illustrative rhetoric

the source recommends making these points to clients during initial discussions as a way of driving home the importance of choosing you as their designer — that is, the premise is also being used as a sales argument, and the source says so

positive.description: Aston Martin versus Škoda; Lexus versus Scion
